heading: Flammable liquids.
title: OSHA flammable liquid storage requirements (29 CFR 1910.106)
description: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.106 flammable liquid storage requirements: tank, piping and container rules, citation data and a printable inspection checklist.
opening: 29 CFR 1910.106 sets OSHA's rules for storing liquids with a flashpoint at or below 199.4 °F (93 °C): how tanks are built, spaced, vented and tested, how piping is made, which containers may hold them, and how ignition sources are controlled.

topIndustries.title: Other Chemical Product and Preparation Manufacturing
Household and Institutional Furniture and Kitchen Cabinet Manufacturing

enforcementSummary: From FY2022 to FY2026 the most-cited paragraphs were (e)(6)(ii) with 281 citations, (e)(9)(iii) with 169 and (d)(2)(i) with 166. (d)(2)(i) is part of the container rules that 1910.106(a)(32) says every flammable liquid container must meet, and the two (e) paragraphs are outside this summary, so read them in the eCFR text. Paragraph (b)(6), the duty to eliminate or control ignition sources where vapors may collect, drew 81 citations, and yearly citations rose from 378 in FY2022 to 476 in FY2025 before falling to 405 in FY2026.
requirementsIntro: 1910.106 covers liquids that meet the flammable liquid definition in 1910.106(a)(19). It is laid out as definitions in (a), tank storage in (b), piping, valves and fittings in (c), container and portable tank storage in (d), then further paragraphs. The groups below give the main rules from (a) to (d)(1). The full eCFR text has more, including the rest of paragraph (d) and everything from (e) onward.

requirements.heading: Which liquids does 1910.106 treat as flammable?
requirements.intro: Under 1910.106(a)(19), a flammable liquid is any liquid with a flashpoint at or below 199.4 °F (93 °C), sorted into four categories by flashpoint and boiling point.

items.text: Category 1 covers liquids with a flashpoint below 73.4 °F (23 °C) and a boiling point at or below 95 °F (35 °C).
Category 2 has the same flashpoint limit as Category 1, but the boiling point is above 95 °F (35 °C).

Category 3 covers flashpoints from 73.4 °F (23 °C) up to and including 140 °F (60 °C). A Category 3 liquid that flashes at 100 °F (37.8 °C) or higher and is heated for use to within 30 °F (16.7 °C) of its flashpoint must be handled under the rules for Category 3 liquids that flash below 100 °F.

Category 4 covers flashpoints above 140 °F (60 °C) and up to 199.4 °F (93 °C). If a Category 4 liquid is heated for use to 30 °F or less below its flashpoint, it is handled as a Category 3 liquid with a flashpoint of 100 °F or higher.
A liquid that flashes above 199.4 °F (93 °C) and is heated for use to within 30 °F of that point must be handled under the Category 4 rules.

requirements.heading: What containers may flammable liquids be stored in?
requirements.intro: 1910.106(a)(32) requires flammable liquids to be stored in a tank or in a container that complies with paragraph (d)(2), and the container rules in paragraph (d) apply within set size limits.

items.text: Keep flammable liquids only in a tank or in a container that meets 1910.106(d)(2).
In this section, a container means any can, barrel or drum.
A safety can is an approved container of 5 gallons or less, with a spring-closing lid and spout cover, designed to relieve internal pressure safely when exposed to fire.
Unless otherwise indicated, approved means approved or listed by a nationally recognized testing laboratory, as defined in 1910.7.
Paragraph (d) applies only to drums and other containers, flammable aerosols included, of no more than 60 gallons each, and to portable tanks of no more than 660 gallons each.

requirements.heading: How must ignition sources and vapors be controlled?
requirements.intro: 1910.106(b)(6) requires employers to take precautions that eliminate or control sources of ignition in locations where flammable vapors may be present.

items.text: Wherever flammable vapor could be present, take precautions to prevent ignition by removing or controlling ignition sources.

The ignition sources the standard names include open flames, lightning, smoking, cutting and welding, hot surfaces, frictional heat, static, electrical and mechanical sparks, spontaneous ignition, chemical and physical-chemical reactions, and radiant heat.
Ventilation counts as adequate under this section when it prevents significant quantities of vapor-air mixture from building up above one-fourth of the lower flammable limit.

For aboveground tanks holding Category 2 liquids, or Category 3 liquids with flashpoints under 100 °F (other than crude oils, gasolines and asphalts), the fill pipe must be designed and installed to minimize static electricity. A fill pipe that enters through the top must end within 6 inches of the tank bottom.

requirements.heading: How far apart must outside aboveground tanks be, and when is a dike needed?
requirements.intro: For outside aboveground tanks, 1910.106(b)(2)(ii) sets a minimum shell-to-shell distance of 3 feet, and 1910.106(b)(2)(vii) requires drainage or a dike around the tanks.

items.text: No two flammable liquid storage tanks may be less than 3 feet apart.

Adjacent tanks must be at least one-sixth of the sum of their diameters apart. Where one tank's diameter is less than half the other's, the gap must be at least half the smaller tank's diameter. Paragraph (b)(2)(ii)(c) allows 3 feet for certain crude petroleum production tanks.
Tanks holding unstable flammable liquids must be separated by at least one-half the sum of their diameters.

Keep liquefied petroleum gas containers at least 20 feet from flammable liquid storage tanks. The paragraph sets exceptions for higher-pressure tanks and for small LPG containers next to small fuel oil tanks.
The area around a tank or group of tanks must be drained or diked so that accidental discharge does not endanger adjoining property or reach waterways.

A diked area must hold at least the greatest amount of liquid that can be released from the largest tank in it, assuming that tank is full. Where several tanks share a dike, subtract the volume of the other tanks below dike height. Paragraph (b)(2)(vii)(c)(2) sets the rule for fixed-roof tanks of crude with boilover characteristics.
Dike walls must be earth, steel, concrete or solid masonry, designed to be liquidtight and to withstand a full hydrostatic head.
Dike walls are limited to an average height of 6 feet above interior grade.
Loose combustible material and drums or barrels, whether empty or full, are not allowed inside the diked area.

requirements.heading: What venting do aboveground tanks need?
requirements.intro: Every aboveground tank needs normal venting under 1910.106(b)(2)(iv) and emergency relief for fire exposure under 1910.106(b)(2)(v).

items.text: Atmospheric tanks must be vented enough to stop filling, emptying and temperature changes from creating vacuum or pressure that would distort a cone roof or exceed the design pressure of other atmospheric tanks.

Normal vents must be sized to API Standard 2000 (1968) or another accepted standard, or be at least as large as the larger of the filling or withdrawal connection. They can never be smaller than 1 1/4 inch nominal inside diameter.

Tanks and pressure vessels holding Category 1 liquids need venting devices that stay closed except when venting under pressure or vacuum. For Category 2 and lower-flashpoint Category 3 liquids, approved flame arresters are an alternative, and (b)(2)(iv)(f)(2) allows open vents on some tanks.
Every aboveground storage tank must have a construction or device that relieves excessive internal pressure caused by an exposure fire.
Each commercial tank venting device must be stamped with its opening pressure, the pressure at which it is fully open, and its flow capacity at that pressure.

Where vents on tanks of Category 1 or 2 liquids, or Category 3 liquids flashing below 100 °F, are next to buildings or public ways, vapors must be released at a safe point outside buildings, 12 feet or more above the adjacent ground.
The same vent outlets must not let vapors be trapped by eaves or other obstructions and must be at least five feet from building openings.

requirements.heading: How must underground tanks be installed?
requirements.intro: 1910.106(b)(3) sets the clearances, bedding, earth cover, corrosion protection and vents for underground tanks.

items.text: A tank storing Category 1 or 2 liquids, or Category 3 liquids below 100 °F flashpoint, must be at least 1 foot from the nearest basement or pit wall and at least 3 feet from a property line that may be built on. Tanks of higher-flashpoint Category 3 or Category 4 liquids need at least 1 foot from a basement, pit or property line.
Set underground tanks on firm foundations, surrounded by at least 6 inches of noncorrosive inert material such as clean sand, earth or gravel, well tamped in place.
Cover tanks with at least 2 feet of earth, or with at least 1 foot of earth topped by a reinforced concrete slab of 4 inches or more.

Tanks that are or may be under traffic need 3 feet of earth, or 18 inches of well-tamped earth plus 6 inches of reinforced concrete or 8 inches of asphaltic concrete. Paving used as protection must extend at least 1 foot beyond the tank outline in all directions.
Protect the tank and its piping against corrosion with coatings or wrappings, cathodic protection, corrosion-resistant materials, or a combination of these.

For tanks holding Category 1 or 2 liquids, or Category 3 liquids with flashpoints under 100 °F, vent pipes must discharge outside buildings, higher than the fill pipe opening and no lower than 12 feet above adjacent ground, pointing upward only.
Fill and discharge lines may enter the tank only through the top, and fill lines must slope toward the tank.

requirements.heading: When may flammable liquid tanks be inside a building?
requirements.intro: 1910.106(b)(4)(i) allows tanks inside buildings only where paragraphs (e), (g), (h) or (i) permit them, and the rest of (b)(4) sets the venting, valve and fill rules for those tanks.

items.text: Vents on indoor tanks must discharge vapors outside the building, and weak roof seams may not be used for emergency venting.
Each connection through which liquid normally flows needs an internal or external valve placed as close as practical to the tank shell.

Each withdrawal connection below the liquid level needs an automatic-closing heat-actuated valve so that flow stops if fire breaks out near the tank. This does not apply to emergency disposal connections, or to one-story buildings designed and protected for flammable liquid storage.
A manual gaging opening that is separate from the fill pipe needs a vaportight cap or cover, plus a spring loaded check valve or other approved device against overflow and vapor release.
The fill pipe inlet must be outside the building, clear of ignition sources and 5 feet or more from any building opening. It must be kept closed and liquidtight when idle and be properly identified.
Indoor tanks must have a device or other means that prevents overflow into the building.

requirements.heading: What supports and tests must tanks have before use?
requirements.intro: Under 1910.106(b)(5) and (b)(7), tanks must sit on firm, fire-protected supports and pass strength and tightness tests before going into service.

items.text: Tank supports must stand on firm foundations and be made of concrete, masonry or protected steel. Single horizontal wood timbers may support outside aboveground tanks if they are no more than 12 inches high at their lowest point.

Steel supports and exposed piling need fire-resistive protection rated at 2 hours or more. Steel saddles under 12 inches high at their lowest point are exempt, and water spray or an equivalent may be used instead.
Tanks in areas that may flood must follow the precautions in 1910.106(b)(5)(vi), which deal with flood stage, water loading, anchoring, valves and structural guides.

Strength-test every tank, shop built or field erected, under the code it was built to before it enters service. An ASME code stamp, API monogram or Underwriters' Laboratories label is evidence of this test.

Test all tanks and connections for tightness. Aboveground tanks are tested at operating pressure with air, inert gas or water. Underground tanks and piping are tested before being covered, either hydrostatically or with air at 3 to 5 pounds per square inch.
Correct all leaks and deformations before the tank enters service. Welded tanks may not be repaired by mechanical caulking, except for pinhole leaks in the roof.

requirements.heading: What does 1910.106 require for piping, valves and fittings?
requirements.intro: 1910.106(c) requires piping systems for flammable liquids to suit the expected working pressures and structural stresses, and sets rules for materials, joints, supports, valves and testing.

items.text: Paragraph (c) does not apply to oil or gas well tubing or casing and piping connected directly to it, to motor vehicle, aircraft, boat or engine systems, or to piping covered by a boiler and pressure vessel code.
Piping, valves and fittings must be steel, nodular iron or malleable iron, unless one of the exceptions in (c)(2)(ii) to (iv) applies.
Joints must be liquid tight, using welded or screwed joints or approved connectors.
Joints that depend on the friction of combustible materials for mechanical continuity may not be used inside buildings.
Support piping systems substantially and protect them from physical damage and from stress caused by settlement, vibration, expansion or contraction.
Paint or otherwise protect piping that is exposed to external corrosion, whether aboveground or underground.
A connection where tank cars or tank vehicles pump liquid into storage tanks needs a check valve against backflow, wherever the piping layout makes backflow possible.

Before piping is covered, enclosed or used, test it hydrostatically to 150 percent of the maximum anticipated system pressure, or pneumatically to 110 percent. The test pressure must be at least 5 pounds per square inch gage at the highest point and held for at least 10 minutes while all joints are visually inspected.

checklistIntro: This checklist covers containers, ignition sources, aboveground, underground and indoor tanks, and piping under 1910.106, for use on a walk-round of any area where flammable liquids are stored.

faq.question: Does paragraph (d) apply to paint kept for maintenance work?
faq.answer: Not if it is kept for 30 days or less. 1910.106(d)(1)(ii)(c) excludes flammable paints, oils, varnishes and similar mixtures used for painting or maintenance when they are not kept longer than 30 days. The same list also excludes container storage in bulk plants, service stations, refineries, chemical plants and distilleries, Category 1, 2 or 3 liquids in the fuel tanks of vehicles, aircraft, boats and engines, and beverages in individual containers of 1 gallon or less.

faq.question: Are flammable aerosols treated as flammable liquids?
faq.answer: For the container storage rules, yes. 1910.106(a)(13) takes the definition of a flammable aerosol from Appendix B to 1910.1200 and says that, for paragraph (d), these aerosols count as Category 1 flammable liquids.

faq.question: What counts as a portable tank?
faq.answer: 1910.106(a)(25) defines a portable tank as a closed container with a liquid capacity over 60 U.S. gallons that is not intended for fixed installation.

faq.question: How does 1910.106 classify tanks by pressure?
faq.answer: An atmospheric tank is designed to operate from atmospheric pressure up to 0.5 p.s.i.g. (1910.106(a)(2)). A low-pressure tank is designed for above 0.5 and up to 15 p.s.i.g. (1910.106(a)(21)). A pressure vessel is designed for above 15 p.s.i.g. (1910.106(a)(26)).
